summary.text: Lesson 3 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words about speech and persuasion (allude, exhort, disseminate), power and loss (subjugate, lament, trauma, implicate), and manner (pensive, stilted, pomp, wanton, feckless), plus consecrate, dote and monetary.

why.text: This set is unusually loaded — most of these words carry a judgement inside them. Learning them is learning to notice when a sentence that looks factual is quietly taking a side.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 3 words correctly
Choose the right sense of a word with several meanings, using context
Name an analogy’s relationship before choosing an answer
Tell words carrying a fixed verdict from words that borrow one

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 3 word list. The analogy questions include the INJURY : TRAUMA example from the book itself — trauma is one of this lesson's words. Wanton is the one to watch: it has three genuinely different senses (immoral, excessive, playful) and the book teaches all three, so a question about it is really asking her to read context first.

nextUp.text: Cards first, then the quiz. On the analogies, say the relationship out loud before you look at the options.

cards.def:
**To refer to something indirectly** (used with *to*). (verb)
• "I made a mistake that night," she said, alluding to losing her temper.
• allusion (n): the indirect reference itself.
cards.hint: Alluding is pointing without naming — if you say it outright, it is not an allusion.

cards.def:
**To set apart as holy; to dedicate to a cause.** (verb)
• Hagia Sophia was consecrated as a church in 537.
• Mother Teresa consecrated her life to helping Calcutta's poor.

**To scatter or spread widely.** (verb)
• The wind disseminated the spores from the milkweed pods.
• dissemination (n): spreading information about flu cases prevents an outbreak.
cards.hint: Semen is Latin for seed — disseminating is sowing seed across a whole field.

cards.def:
**To show excessive fondness for** (used with *on* or *upon*). (verb)
• She dotes on her grandson and indulges his every whim.
• The excess is the point — doting is fondness past the sensible line.

**To urge strongly; to warn or appeal.** (verb)
• The quarterback's teammate exhorted him to ignore the boos of the crowd.
• exhortation (n): the pool rules contain an exhortation against diving in the shallow end.

**Careless or irresponsible.** (adjective)
• Bao's feckless ways left him devoid of cash.
• Feck is an old word for effect — a feckless person has no effect on anything.

**To show to be involved with something, especially something dishonest or illegal.** (verb)
• The defence attorney insisted her client could not be implicated in the theft.
• Being implicated is not being convicted — it means the evidence points your way.

**To feel or express grief.** (verb)
• Mourners lined the streets to lament the death of Diana, Princess of Wales.
• lamentation (n): an expression of grief in the form of a poem or song.

**Of or relating to money or currency.** (adjective)
• The basic monetary unit of Mexico is the peso.
• Reach for it when the subject is money as a SYSTEM, not just a price.

**Deep in thought; dreamily thoughtful.** (adjective)
• Lying on my back, I grew pensive as I watched the drifting summer clouds.
• Pensive thought drifts — it is not the same as concentrating.

**A showy or dignified display.** (noun)
• Graduations are usually marked by pomp and ceremony.
• Pomp can be admiring or mocking depending on who is describing it.

**Artificially stiff or formal in manner.** (adjective)
• His stilted conversation reflected his unease.
• Think of walking on stilts: upright, careful, and obviously not natural.

**To bring under control; to conquer.** (verb)
• In the late eighteenth century, Russia subjugated Georgia and absorbed it into its empire.
• subjugation (n): the subjugation of the working class has driven revolutions worldwide.

**A severe bodily injury.** (noun)
• Second meaning: emotional shock — survivors experienced trauma for years after the tornado.
• traumatic (adj): watching the devastation on television had a traumatic effect on me.

**Ignoring what is right.** (adjective)
• The company showed a wanton disregard for employees' health by leaving the asbestos.
• Also: excessive and unrestrained (wanton eating of sweets), or simply playful (wanton shouts of children).
cards.hint: Three shades, from cruel to merely playful. The context picks which one.

questions.q: To allude to something is to:
opts: Spread it widely to many people
questions.hint: The word points at something without naming it.
steps: Allude means to refer to something in an indirect way.
Saying "I made a mistake that night" ALLUDES to losing your temper without describing it.
Stating it plainly is the opposite move; the other options define disseminate and consecrate.

ex.main: **To refer to it indirectly.** The indirectness is the whole word — name the thing and you have stopped alluding.
ex.tip: An allusion asks the listener to supply the missing half. That is why writers use them and why tests ask about them.

steps: Feckless means careless or irresponsible.
Bao's feckless ways leaving him without cash shows carelessness producing consequences.
The wrong options define stilted, pensive and flamboyant.

ex.main: **Careless and irresponsible.** Feck is an old word for effect — the feckless produce none.
ex.tip: Old roots hiding in modern words are worth learning once: they unlock the word permanently.

questions.q: To subjugate a people is to:
opts: Bring them under control by conquest
questions.hint: Look at the "sub" — it means under.
steps: Subjugate means to bring under control; to conquer.
Russia subjugating Georgia meant conquering it and absorbing it into the empire.
Setting free is emancipate — the exact reverse.

ex.main: **Bring them under control by conquest.** Sub- means under; subjugation puts a people under a yoke.
ex.tip: Subjugate and emancipate are opposites and both appear on tests. Learn them facing each other.

questions.q: A pensive expression suggests someone is:
questions.hint: It is a quiet, inward look.
steps: Pensive means deep in thought, in a dreamy rather than intense way.
Watching clouds drift and growing pensive is the word in its natural habitat.
None of the other options involves thinking at all.

ex.main: **Deep in thought.** Pensive thought wanders; it is reflection rather than concentration.
ex.tip: Two words can both mean "thinking" and still not swap: pensive drifts, focused drills.

opts: The reward was monetary rather than a trophy or a certificate
She gave a monetary glance at the clock
The monetary hike took us four hours
He has a monetary interest in old films
steps: Monetary means of or relating to money or currency.
A reward that is money rather than a trophy is exactly a monetary reward.
Glances, hikes and interests in films have nothing to do with currency.

ex.main: **The reward was money rather than an object.** Monetary attaches to systems, values and rewards — not to moods or motions.
ex.tip: When only one option can literally involve money, the definition alone settles the question.

questions.q: What does it mean to disseminate information?
questions.hint: Think of seeds scattered by the wind.
steps: Disseminate means to scatter or spread widely.
The wind disseminating milkweed spores is the literal picture behind the word.
Applied to information it means spreading it broadly — the opposite of keeping it secret.

ex.main: **To spread it widely.** Dissemination of flu information is how an outbreak gets prevented.
ex.tip: A word with a physical origin usually keeps that motion when it turns abstract. Picture the seeds.

questions.q: A newspaper reports that a witness "implicated" a company executive. This means the witness:
opts: Gave evidence suggesting the executive was involved in wrongdoing
Proved the executive guilty beyond doubt
Defended the executive against the accusations
questions.hint: Implicate points; it does not convict.
steps: To implicate is to show someone to be involved in something dishonest or illegal.
It means the evidence points toward that person.
It stops well short of proof — which is why newspapers use it rather than "proved guilty".

ex.main: **Evidence suggesting involvement — not proof of guilt.** That gap is exactly why the word is useful to careful reporters.
ex.tip: Legal vocabulary is precise about certainty. Implicated, charged, and convicted are three very different claims.

questions.q: A critic writes that the dialogue in a play was "stilted throughout." The critic means the dialogue:
opts: Sounded artificially stiff and formal rather than natural
Was too fast for the audience to follow
Contained too many references to other plays
questions.hint: Would real people talk that way?
steps: Stilted means artificially stiff or formal in manner.
Applied to dialogue it means the lines do not sound like speech.
Speed, allusions and improvisation are all different complaints.

ex.main: **Artificially stiff, not how people actually speak.** Stilted is always a criticism — nobody aims for it.
ex.tip: For words that are always negative, the question is usually not "what does it mean" but "what is being criticized".

questions.q: Which sentence uses wanton in its "ignoring what is right" sense?
opts: The report described the wanton destruction of protected forest
The children ran across the field with wanton delight
She avoided wanton snacking between meals
The wanton stream wound slowly through the valley
questions.hint: Wanton has three shades. Which sentence carries moral weight?
steps: Wanton can mean ignoring what is right, excessive, or simply playful.
Destruction of PROTECTED forest carries moral weight — someone ignored what was right.
The children's delight is the playful sense; snacking is the excessive sense; a stream cannot be any of them.

ex.main: **The destruction of protected forest.** Only that sentence involves a wrong being ignored.
ex.tip: When a word has several senses, decide which one the SENTENCE needs before deciding whether it fits.

questions.hint: A trauma is not just any injury. How much more is it?
steps: Work out the stem: a trauma is a SEVERE injury — the second word is the intense version of the first.
So the pattern is degree, running from ordinary up to extreme.
Adoration is intense fondness — same direction, same jump. Match.
Consecrate and profane are opposites, pensive and thoughtful are near-synonyms, and monetary is simply the adjective of money.

ex.main: **Both pairs are DEGREE: the second word is the extreme form of the first.** Injury to trauma is the same jump as fondness to adoration.
ex.tip: Degree pairs have a direction. Check that your answer runs the SAME way — mild to intense, not intense to mild.

questions.hint: These two words mean nearly the same thing.
steps: To disseminate is to scatter or spread widely — the two words are near-synonyms.
So the relationship is simply: same meaning.
To exhort is to urge strongly. Same meaning. Match.
Subjugate and liberate are opposites, trauma intensifies injury, and pomp is a kind of ceremonial display.

ex.main: **Both pairs are SYNONYMS.** Disseminate and scatter overlap; so do exhort and urge.
ex.tip: Synonym stems are the easiest to spot and the easiest to over-trust — always confirm no option is a BETTER synonym.

questions.hint: What quality is a wanton person missing?
steps: In its "excessive" sense, wanton means lacking restraint — the adjective names what is ABSENT.
So the pattern is: adjective : the quality it lacks.
Feckless means lacking responsibility. Same pattern. Match.
Monetary relates to money, consecrate and dedicate are synonyms, and lament expresses grief — relating, matching and expressing are not lacking.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ADJECTIVE : THE QUALITY IT LACKS.** Wanton behaviour has no restraint; feckless behaviour has no responsibility.
ex.tip: A "lacks" relationship is easy to miss because it looks like an ordinary pairing. Ask whether the second word is present or absent.

questions.hint: What is a person doing to grief when they lament?
steps: To lament is to EXPRESS grief — the verb puts the emotion outward.
So the pattern is: verb : the emotion it expresses.
To celebrate is to express joy. Match.
Subjugating removes freedom, pensive and quiet are both adjectives, and doting is the opposite of neglect.

ex.main: **Both pairs are VERB EXPRESSES EMOTION.** Lamenting puts grief outward; celebrating puts joy outward.
ex.tip: Verb-plus-emotion pairs split into expressing, causing and removing. Naming which one you have is the whole question.

questions.q: A historian writes: "The victors consecrated the ground where the defenders had been subjugated." What tension does this sentence create?
opts: A place is being called holy precisely where people were conquered
The victors are admitting they lost the battle
The ground was too damaged to be used again
The defenders were the ones who performed the ceremony
questions.hint: Look at what each verb means, then notice they land on the same ground.
steps: Consecrate means to set apart as holy.
Subjugate means to bring under control by conquest.
The sentence puts both on the same spot: the victors sanctify the site of a conquest.
That is the tension — holiness claimed over a place defined by someone else's defeat.

ex.main: **Sacred ground declared on the site of a conquest.** The sentence does not say this is wrong; it lets the two words sit against each other and lets you notice.
ex.tip: Historians often build an argument by word choice alone. When two loaded verbs share a sentence, ask what their collision implies.

questions.q: Which pairing shows the SAME word being used approvingly by one speaker and critically by another?
opts: pomp — "the pomp of the ceremony" versus "all that empty pomp"
trauma — used the same way by everyone
questions.hint: Which word can swing either way depending on the speaker?
steps: Pomp means a showy or dignified display — and dignity and showiness are judged differently by different people.
"The pomp of the ceremony" admires it; "all that empty pomp" dismisses it as hollow.
Feckless is always critical, monetary is neutral, and trauma is not a judgement at all.

ex.main: **Pomp swings with the speaker.** The word describes the display; the speaker supplies the verdict.
ex.tip: Some words carry a fixed verdict and some borrow one from context. Knowing which is which keeps you from misreading tone.

questions.q: To consecrate a building is to:
opts: Sell it to the highest bidder
questions.hint: It is a religious or dedicating act.
steps: Consecrate means to set apart as holy, or to dedicate to a cause.
Hagia Sophia was consecrated as a church in 537 — set apart for sacred use.
None of the other options involves dedication of any kind.

ex.main: **Set it apart as holy.** The second sense extends it to causes: Mother Teresa consecrated her life to the poor.
ex.tip: A word with a sacred sense and a secular one usually keeps the same feeling in both: consecrating a life is still setting it apart.

questions.q: A novelist writes that a father "doted on" his youngest child. The word choice suggests the father was:
opts: Fond of the child past the point of good judgement
Strict with the child but fair
Largely absent from the child’s life
questions.hint: Dote is fondness with a word of warning built in.
steps: Dote means to show EXCESSIVE fondness for someone.
The excess is part of the definition, not an accident of tone.
So describing a father as doting says he indulged the child beyond what was wise.
Disappointment, strictness and absence are all the opposite of doting.

ex.main: **Fond past the point of good judgement.** Doting is affection the writer is gently flagging as too much.
ex.tip: When a definition contains a word like "excessive", the criticism travels with the word wherever it goes.

questions.q: A speaker "alluded to" a scandal; a second speaker "exhorted" the audience about it. What is the difference in what each did?
opts: The first referred to it indirectly; the second urged the audience strongly
The first proved it happened; the second denied it
The first spoke privately; the second spoke publicly
The first grieved over it; the second celebrated it
questions.hint: One word is about indirectness, the other about force.
steps: To allude is to refer to something indirectly, without naming it outright.
To exhort is to urge strongly — an appeal aimed at getting the audience to act or believe.
So the first speaker gestured at the scandal; the second pressed the audience about it.
The difference is manner and force, not truth, privacy or emotion.

ex.main: **Indirect reference versus strong urging.** Allude is about how much is said; exhort is about how hard it is pushed.
ex.tip: Verbs of speaking are worth sorting on two axes: how direct the speaker is, and how hard they are pushing.
